about.title: Temecula Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely feels like a legal matter in the moment. You're picking yourself up off a wet grocery aisle near Winchester Road, or catching your breath after a broken step at an apartment complex off Margarita Road, and the first thought is usually embarrassment rather than evidence. Premises liability claims in California turn on notice: whether the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and did nothing to fix it or warn you. That means photos of the spill, the lighting, the missing handrail, or the uneven pavement are worth taking right away, and store surveillance footage should be requested before it gets recorded over. Temecula is home to roughly 112,000 residents, with busy retail stretches along Rancho California Road and Winchester Road where parking lots and storefronts see steady foot traffic. LawProactive is not a law firm. We're a free service that connects you with an independent attorney in Riverside County who takes these claims on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Temecula Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Attorneys who understand the notice requirement
items.desc: California asks you to show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The independent attorneys in our network know how to gather inspection logs, cleaning schedules, and prior complaints that speak to that question.

items.title: Help preserving video before it disappears
items.desc: Many Temecula shopping centers and apartment complexes record over surveillance footage within days or weeks. Connecting with an attorney early means a preservation letter can go out while the video still exists.

items.title: Clear guidance on deadlines and shared fault
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but far less if a public entity owns the property, and California's pure comparative fault rule means a claim can still move forward even if you were partly to blame.

items.question: I fell on a public sidewalk or in a city park in Temecula. Does the same two-year deadline apply?
items.answer: Not usually. When the property belongs to a public entity such as the City of Temecula, Riverside County, or the state, California generally requires a government claim to be filed within six months of the injury, well before any lawsuit. Missing that window can end the claim entirely, so it's worth talking to an attorney quickly to sort out who actually owns and maintains the spot where you fell.

items.question: The store says I wasn't watching where I was going. Can I still bring a claim?
items.answer: Possibly. California follows pure comparative fault, which means a jury can assign a percentage of responsibility to you and still hold the property owner accountable for their share. Your recovery would be reduced by your percentage, not eliminated. An independent attorney can look at the facts, including whether the hazard was hidden or unmarked, before anyone accepts a store's version of events.

items.question: What should I do in the first few days after a fall at a business in Temecula?
items.answer: Get medical care first, then photograph the hazard, the surrounding area, and your shoes and clothing if they're relevant. Ask the business for a written incident report and request, in writing, that they preserve any surveillance video from that day. If you'd like help, LawProactive can connect you at no cost with an independent attorney who can send a formal preservation demand on your behalf.
